tldr: Homeland Security ordered DeepSeek stripped out of every federal civilian agency, including third-party tools built on its models.
France imposed curfews on central Paris, Lille and other cities after more than 2,300 arrests over the weekend.
Korea's Elice fell as much as 37% on debut despite 408x retail demand, and SoftBank's credit risk hit a four-year high.
Trump ordered a women's health division at NIH within 90 days and revoked Biden's 2024 research order.
Alberta voted 76.4% to stay in Canada, rejecting even a first step toward secession.
Anthropic pledged 5% of its shares to a public benefit fund; Musk countered with a SpaceX share for every American child.
Traders put a December Fed hike at 89% with the 10-year Treasury near 5.1% and September CPI at 3.7%.
Qatar said it will unveil a Gulf defence pact covering air, drone and cyber defence, with no members named yet.
A 16-year-old Broadcom Wi-Fi flaw gives root on routers from radio range, and Broadcom will not issue a CVE.
Trump claimed a 25-to-30-point Kansas margin at a Kansas rally; his best there was 20.6 points.

items.headline: Homeland Security orders DeepSeek removed from every federal civilian agency
items.body: The Department of Homeland Security published Exclusion and Removal Order #2026-01 in the Federal Register on Monday, barring civilian agencies from buying or running anything from Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co. and requiring them to remove what is already installed. Secretary Markwayne Mullin signed it under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018, citing data flowing to Chinese servers; it also reaches third-party products "developed using DeepSeek implementations." Outlets disagree on the signing date: Bloomberg reports July 24, surfacing only now, while CyberScoop cites June 26.
items.plain: DeepSeek is a Chinese company that publishes its models' weights, the numbers that make an AI model work, so anyone can download them and build products on top. That is what makes this ban awkward to enforce. Blocking an app is simple; blocking a model already buried inside other vendors' software means agencies have to audit what their suppliers built with. The 2018 law being used here lets a single department order a supplier out of government systems without any vote in Congress. It does not touch private companies or consumers.
items.why: Open weights were supposed to make a model impossible to ban, so the government is banning the procurement chain instead, which shifts the burden onto every vendor that quietly built on Chinese models.

items.headline: France imposes curfews on central Paris and a string of cities after a weekend of riots
items.body: Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu asked local authorities on Monday to impose partial curfews after weeks of high-school protests over school conditions and living costs escalated into looting and arson. The Interior Ministry said more than 2,300 people were arrested over the weekend and almost 1,000 police and gendarmes were injured on Saturday alone. Curfews now cover Place de la Republique and Les Halles in Paris from 11pm to 6am, plus Lille, Douai, Wattignies and Denain. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said police had "lost control" in several cities.
items.plain: French high-school students, the lyceens, began protesting over understaffed and unrepaired schools, and the anger widened into a general complaint about living costs. A curfew is an order that nobody may be outdoors in a named area between set hours, which lets police clear a street without first deciding who is protesting and who is looting. The political catch: Lecornu's government has no majority in parliament, so it is reaching for police powers because it cannot pass laws. Some coverage reports two deaths; most outlets do not, so treat that as unconfirmed.
items.why: A government with no parliamentary majority has defaulted to curfews eighteen months before a presidential election, which hands the National Rally the argument that the centre cannot keep order.

items.headline: An AI data-centre listing collapses on its first day as SoftBank's credit risk hits a four-year high
items.body: Elice, a South Korean AI data-centre operator, raised 201.1 billion won ($151 million) at the top of its range after retail orders came in 408 times oversubscribed, then opened 16% below the offer price on Tuesday and traded as much as 37% down. The same morning SoftBank's five-year credit default swap spread reached 432 basis points, its highest since November 2022. Nscale has met investor resistance to a New York listing target reported between $30 billion and $35 billion, and Firmus withdrew its IPO this month.
items.plain: A credit default swap is insurance against a company failing to pay its debts, so when its price jumps, lenders are nervous. SoftBank has borrowed heavily to fund roughly $64.6 billion of commitments to OpenAI. The Elice debut matters less for the size of the fall than for how it happened: demand was enormous while the price was fixed, and collapsed the moment real buyers set it. Data centres cost money up front and earn it back over a decade, and at a 5% Treasury yield that wait got expensive.
items.why: Investors are not refusing to fund AI infrastructure; they are refusing to fund it at the prices builders assumed, which is how a boom decelerates without anyone announcing it.

items.headline: Trump creates a women's health division at NIH and revokes Biden's research order
items.body: Trump signed an executive order on Monday directing the Department of Health and Human Services to establish a women's health division inside the National Institutes of Health within 90 days, and creating a White House task force co-chaired by chief of staff Susie Wiles and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., which met the same day. Named priorities include maternal health, mental health, endometriosis and using artificial intelligence to speed discovery. The order revokes Biden's 2024 executive order and memorandum on the same subject. No research funding figure was disclosed, and the division does not replace NIH's existing Office of Research on Women's Health.
items.plain: NIH is the US government's main funder of medical research, handing out tens of billions of dollars a year. Women were historically underrepresented in clinical trials, so conditions such as endometriosis, in which tissue resembling the uterine lining grows outside the uterus, remain poorly understood. A new division can set priorities, but priorities without a budget line do not move money, and only Congress appropriates it. That is the gap in this order: it names diseases and a 90-day deadline and says nothing about dollars, while cancelling the previous order on the same subject.
items.why: Whether this is an expansion or a relabelling turns on a funding number the White House has not published, and that number is one Congress controls rather than the president.

items.headline: Alberta votes 76% to stay in Canada, rejecting a first step toward secession
items.body: Albertans rejected a move toward independence in Monday's non-binding referendum, with early unofficial counts at 76.4% for remaining in Canada and 23.6% for beginning the legal process toward a later, binding separation vote. Pre-referendum polling had put the remain side between roughly 66% and 74%, so the margin ran ahead of expectations. Prime Minister Mark Carney said "Albertans made a clear choice," adding, "Above all, Albertans chose Canada." Separatist organisers said the movement will continue.
items.plain: Alberta is Canada's oil province, and its long-standing grievance is that Ottawa taxes and regulates the industry while much of the revenue flows east. The ballot did not ask whether to leave the country; it asked whether to start the legal process for a future binding vote, which is a deliberately low-stakes first step. That is what makes 76% decisive: voters declined even to open the door. Canadian polling had shown this much closer, which suggests people tell pollsters they are angry more readily than they vote to leave.
items.why: A defeat this lopsided removes secession as a credible threat in Alberta's bargaining with Ottawa over pipelines and emissions rules, which was the leverage the referendum was meant to create.

items.headline: Anthropic pledges 5% of its shares to a public benefit fund, and Musk answers with a SpaceX share for every American child
items.body: Anthropic said on Sunday it will commit 5% of its stock, subject to shareholder approval, to a wholly owned limited liability company structured as a public benefit fund, with the board able to add 2% more for every 50% rise in company value above an undisclosed baseline. The equity cannot be used for lobbying or political giving. On Monday Elon Musk posted that he would instead give one of his SpaceX shares "to every kid in America" next year, worth roughly $10.5 billion across about 72 million children, possibly through the Treasury's Trump Accounts. Neither plan has published its mechanics.
items.plain: A public benefit fund here is not a charity. It is a company Anthropic owns, holding Anthropic shares, which the firm says it will use for public purposes later. That is why the governance details matter more than the 5%: who controls the fund, and what valuation triggers release more stock, have not been disclosed. Musk's version skips the middle step by handing shares to people directly, but a share in a private company cannot easily be sold, so the $10.5 billion is a paper figure until SpaceX lists publicly.
items.why: Both pledges land while AI firms face public anger over job losses, and neither is binding yet, which makes them a test of whether an equity promise counts as accountability.

items.headline: Traders now put a December Fed rate rise at 89%, with the 10-year Treasury near 5.1%
items.body: The 10-year Treasury yield sat around 5.08% on Tuesday, a week before the Federal Open Market Committee meets on October 27 and 28. CME FedWatch pricing gives an October increase about a 15% chance and a December increase about 89%, after September consumer prices rose 3.7% from a year earlier, up from 3.4% in August, and wholesale prices rose 6.3%, the largest annual gain since 2022. Chair Kevin Warsh said "I don't prejudge meetings" in Bangkok on Friday.
items.plain: The Federal Reserve sets a short-term interest rate to control inflation; raising it makes borrowing dearer, which cools spending and prices. It is raising rates now rather than cutting, which tells you inflation has not come down. The 10-year Treasury yield matters more to everyday life than the Fed's own rate, because mortgages and corporate loans are priced off it. At roughly 5%, any project built on the assumption of cheap money, data centres very much included, has to earn considerably more to be worth building.
items.why: A December increase has moved from a risk to the market's base case, which has already repriced mortgages and capital spending before the Fed has taken a vote.

items.headline: Qatar says it will announce a regional defence pact built around air and drone defence
items.body: Deputy Prime Minister Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani told the Global Security Forum in Doha on Monday that Qatar will unveil a regional defence partnership covering air defence, counter-drone systems, cyber security and electronic warfare, alongside a local arms-production hub involving the United States, Britain and France. No member states have been named and no text has been published. He also called for talks and closer economic ties with Iran, and warned that the region's energy disruption has not yet peaked.
items.plain: Gulf states have spent decades buying weapons from the West rather than building a shared defence, partly because they do not entirely trust one another. The Iran war changed that: missiles and cheap drones crossed borders, and Riyadh's main airport has been shut for days after a Houthi strike. Counter-drone defence is the gap, because shooting down a $20,000 drone with a $2 million interceptor is a losing trade. Note the sequence: Qatar has announced that it will announce something, with no members and no document.
items.why: A Gulf air-defence bloc assembled by a state that is simultaneously courting Tehran hedges against both Iranian missiles and an unreliable American guarantee, which inverts how Washington has organised the region.

items.headline: A 16-year-old Broadcom Wi-Fi bug hands over routers from radio range, and there is no patch
items.body: Researcher Quentin Kaiser disclosed a flaw he calls WPSplinter at the Hexacon conference in Paris on October 16: Broadcom's legacy Wi-Fi Protected Setup code fails to check the size of reassembled EAP-WPS message fragments against its destination buffer, letting anyone within radio range run code as root on a router with no network password, PIN or button press. Kaiser traces the code to at least 2010 and says Broadcom shipped an incomplete fix in 2018 without public disclosure. Broadcom has declined to assign a CVE identifier, no public patch exists, and vendors shipping affected chips include Cisco, TP-Link, Netgear, Nokia and ZTE.
items.plain: WPS is the convenience feature that lets you join a Wi-Fi network by pressing a button on the router instead of typing a password. The bug sits in the code that listens for those requests, and that code listens before anyone has proved who they are, which is why no password is needed. Root means complete control of the device. A CVE is the public tracking number security tools rely on; without one, scanners do not know to look. Turning WPS off does not reliably help. Kaiser says he has seen no exploitation in the wild.
items.why: The missing CVE is the durable part of this story: a vendor can keep a flaw off every patch dashboard and vulnerability scanner simply by declining to number it.

items.headline: Trump overstates his Kansas margin while standing in Kansas, and renews a $5,000 promise with no bill behind it
items.body: Campaigning for Senator Roger Marshall at the Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City, Kansas, on Monday, Trump said he had carried the state by 25 to 30 points. His largest Kansas margin was 20.6 points, and his vote share across 2016, 2020 and 2024 ran between 56.2% and 57.1%. He renewed his pledge to send every American adult $5,000 if Republicans hold both chambers in November, putting the cost near $1 trillion; Census figures imply roughly $1.2 trillion, and Penn Wharton's Kent Smetters estimated $1.35 trillion. No bill has been introduced. The Kansas Reflector also rated false his claim that the law requires doctors to pursue patients' medical debt.
items.plain: A margin is the gap between the winner's and the loser's share of the vote, and Kansas's results are a matter of public record, so 20.6 points is not an estimate or a disputed poll. The $5,000 promise is conditional twice over: on an election outcome, and on money Congress has not appropriated, since a president cannot send cheques without a law. Two similar pledges in 2025, a "DOGE dividend" and a $2,000 tariff rebate, were never paid. A Reuters/Ipsos poll found 63% of Americans rejected the idea.
items.why: Each of the three cash-payment promises since 2025 has been contingent on something the president does not control, and the appropriation needed to honour this one has not been requested.
